messages.subject: Issue with smaller sample set (k=1?)
messages.subject_clean: Issue with smaller sample set (k=1?)
messages.body_plain:
Hello there!

I am attempting to use codex to analyze a sample set and have been running into the following problem:

Getting coverage for sample: read length 75.

Excluded 39 exons due to extreme coverage.

Excluded 5 exons due to extreme exonic length.

Excluded 10 exons due to extreme mappability.

Excluded 3 exons due to extreme GC content.

After taking union, excluded 52 out of 1260 exons in QC.

k = 1

Error in (Y_qc/(fhatnew * Nmat * exp(ghat %*% t(hhat))))[, normal_index] :

  subscript out of bounds

Calls: normalize2 -> apply

Execution halted

After reading around on these forums I have discovered someone else encountered a different error at the same step of the program run:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/codex_wes_cnv/Error$20in$20(Y_qc$2F(fhatnew$20*$20Nmat$20*$20exp(ghat$20$25*$25$20t(hhat))))%5B$2C$20normal_index%5D$20$3A%7Csort:relevance/codex_wes_cnv/swd-PwTF7Lw/fA4NKVeTbfsJ

It appears their error was due to a low k value; this set of samples contains fewer than those I have previously run with Codex and I am wondering if you knew whether this is perhaps resulting in fewer principal components/lower value of k and thus creating a similar error as the other user?

Thank you for your time!

messages.subject: Re: questions for CODEX package
messages.subject_clean: questions for CODEX package
messages.body_plain:
Hi Yaxun,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX. CODEX by default uses hg19 as reference. You can however adapt it to hg38 instead. To do so you need to download the package https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/data/annotation/html/BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38.html . After loading CODEX, you need to load this package so that the Hsapiens by CODEX (hg19) is masked as hg38.

The reference is only used to calculate the GC content. Mappability is bit more complicated and takes longer to run. For CODEX, we pre-compute the mappability for all exonic regions in hg19. For your case, I recommend setting all mappability to 1. That is, mapp=rep(1,length(gc)). Mappability is only used in the QC procedure so this shouldn’t affect your final output too much. If you want, you can also perform QC based on annotation results, i.e., you can remove all exons within segmental duplication regions, which generally have low mappability.

I hope that this helps and feel free to let me know if you have more questions.

Yuchao

Hi,

Do you have suggestions for analysing CNVs from mitochondrial DNA with CODEX? I have files from targeted sequencing for mitochondrial DNA. For now I keep running into errors, and try to solve them one by one. The latest I couldn't solve, from the getmapp.R function

I have successfully used CODEX for targeted gene panel analysis, and I like it very much and would like to be able to continue doing analysis with it.

Best regards
Salla Välipakka

messages.subject_clean: [codex_wes_cnv] Mitochondrial DNA analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Salla,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX. This is the first time I got an email asking about application of CODEX to mt genome, which is interesting and I hope CODEX can be of help.
For CODEX, we pre-calculate all mappability for the autosome and sex chromosome since it can be time-consuming.
For your case, you can set all mappability to 1. That is, mapp=rep(1, length(gc)) after calculating the GC content. The mappability is only used in the QC step and thus this should not affect your final output.

What you need to be careful about is the calculation of the GC content since this is used as input for normalization to get the GC content bias. I recommend some sanity check and zooming in the the function getgc(), which is very short to read.

Let me know if you have further questions.
Yuchao

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

First, I would like say that I really like CODEX and our tests performed on a large clinical cohort confirmed it's superiority over other approaches.

Currently, we are doing some metanalysis and benchmark of few CNV callers and we have a question regarding supplementary table S4 from your CODEX manuscript.
We tried to recompute some of evaluation metrics (including TP, FP, TN, FN)  based on raw data you provided in other supplemental files.
We expected that in case of CODEX algorithm and HAPMAP reference data set (all samples included in HAPMAP were processed by CODEX) the number of TPs + FPs should be equal to the total number of calls returned by CODEX, i.e. 1806 calls (as reported in Table 1).
However, in supplementary table S4 there are 377 TPs  and 255 FPs, which is much smaller than 1806.

Could you please, explain how did you calculated the number of TPs, FPs, TNs and FNs?  In particular, did you performed any additional filtering, i.e. by CNV length, type?
I am sorry if I missed something.

Many thanks,
Tomasz Gambin

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tomasz,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX and I’m glad it’s working well.

For your questions with regard to Supplementary Table S4, the total number of calls reported in Table 1 are from CODEX’s run across all the chromosomes. However, not all of the CNVs overlap with the CNVs reported by microarray-based studies, which we used as “gold standards”. Therefore, in this table we only report the CNVs with confirmed microarray calls, which is summarized in Supplementary Table S3.

I hope this answers your question. FYI, we’ve also carried out additional benchmarking using this same dataset. We find that not all of the ”gold-standard" CNVs in supplementary Table S3 are reliable and should be filtered through QC based on, e.g., length, annotation results (whether overlap with segmental duplication regions, etc).

Feel free to let us know if you have additional questions.

Cheers,
Yuchao

messages.body_plain:
"In your case, I understand you considered only CODEX calls that have at least some overlap with at least one HAPMAP CNV (possibly in other sample). Am I right?"

This is correct. Essentially not all 1806 calls by CODEX overlap with HapMap CNV calls, same with other three methods too. We treat HapMap CNV calls as gold standards -- the ones called by CODEX that don't overlap with the gold standards cannot be categorized as FP, TP, TN, or FN. This has been a long time, but what we did should be: (1) first filter out all CODEX, XHMM, etc.'s  calls that don't overlap with any HapMap calls, (2) for those that do overlap, we attribute them to FP, TP, TN, or FN and then calculate the precision and recall.

To filtering on the gold standard CNV calls we have include: (1) overlap with at least 2 and at most 20 exons. (2) with NA rates less than 5% (some samples have NA from HapMap microarray calls) (3) number of CNV states <=3 (4) CNV rate less than 90% with at least one non-null sample (since we only have 90 samples, for some microarray calls from all cohort the 90 samples are all copy-number-neutral); (5) not overlap with previously reported seg dup region.

Hope this clarifies!
Yuchao

> "In your case, I understand you considered only CODEX calls that have at least some overlap with at least one HAPMAP CNV (possibly in other sample). Am I right?"
>
> This is correct. Essentially not all 1806 calls by CODEX overlap with HapMap CNV calls, same with other three methods too. We treat HapMap CNV calls as gold standards -- the ones called by CODEX that don't overlap with the gold standards cannot be categorized as FP, TP, TN, or FN. This has been a long time, but what we did should be: (1) first filter out all CODEX, XHMM, etc.'s  calls that don't overlap with any HapMap calls, (2) for those that do overlap, we attribute them to FP, TP, TN, or FN and then calculate the precision and recall.
>
> To filtering on the gold standard CNV calls we have include: (1) overlap with at least 2 and at most 20 exons. (2) with NA rates less than 5% (some samples have NA from HapMap microarray calls) (3) number of CNV states <=3 (4) CNV rate less than 90% with at least one non-null sample (since we only have 90 samples, for some microarray calls from all cohort the 90 samples are all copy-number-neutral); (5) not overlap with previously reported seg dup region.
>
> Hope this clarifies!
> Yuchao

Dear Maely,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX. You can use the codes under “CODEX for targeted sequencing” from our GitHub page https://github.com/yuchaojiang/CODEX to adapt CODEX for targeted sequencing. Note that if you have case control experimental design, for the normalization step you need to use normalize2() with normal_index specifying the sample indices for the normal samples. If all samples are all germline, you can use the default normalize() function.

Feel free to let us know if you have any further questions.

Cheers,
Yuchao
